entries.note: “Mediocre” is an assessment of quality without an agreed standard.
The proposition changes “most likely to benefit” into actually benefiting most.

entries.test: Public benchmark contamination experiments and comparisons of benchmark gains with independent task performance would test gaming and whether scores reliably demonstrate progress.
GPT-4.5's published SimpleQA results and evaluated answers would establish its error rate and whether those errors were confidently fabricated answers.
entries.note: A wrong answer does not automatically establish confident fabrication.

entries.test: Controlled experiments training models on known SimpleQA answers would establish whether that intervention inflates their benchmark scores.
entries.note: This asserts a demonstrable mechanism, rather than speculating that a vendor actually cheated.

entries.test: Published benchmark auditing rules, enforcement records, and documented cheating in high-stakes honor systems would test these assertions.
Representative public ChatGPT usage studies compared with SimpleQA's discrete factual questions would establish whether that format represents most usage.
entries.note: The source addresses SimpleQA; the proposition broadens this to OpenAI's hallucination testing generally.

entries.test: Public experiments on contamination or answer-specific training for IMO evaluations would establish their susceptibility to benchmark exploitation.
Public product releases and technical documentation would establish whether the cited improvements from larger models produced products by publication.
entries.note: “Meaningful” introduces a qualification absent from the source's assertion that these results have not led to products.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and independent evaluations available by publication would establish whether any system demonstrated general human-level intelligence and capability.

entries.note: “AI doesn't work” identifies neither a task nor a shared criterion for success.
“Cowardice” functions as a polemical insult.
The proposition removes “a kind of” and changes unwillingness to admit something into a prediction that nobody will admit it.

entries.test: Following the end of tech hyper-growth, public valuation, employment, and regional economic data would establish the predicted crash, layoffs, and historically unprecedented prolonged downturn.
entries.note: No deadline is stated.

entries.test: Major technology companies' public financial disclosures and spending reports would establish whether their cumulative generative AI expenditure reached hundreds of billions by publication.
entries.note: “Real artificial intelligence” replaces the source's comparison with popular expectations. The expenditure assertion is independently testable.

entries.test: Public generative AI revenue, costs, financing needs, and corporate growth strategies would test the asserted commercial losses and dependence on continued subsidy.
entries.note: Questionable usefulness is evaluative, but the financial and commercial assertions have a testable reading.

entries.test: OpenAI's reported 2024 cash burn, the announced funding round, and SoftBank's financing disclosures would establish the stated amounts and funding shares.
Public financial reports, profitability projections, and evidence of sustained mass-market use would test the claimed losses, limited returns, and absence of a mass-market use case.
entries.note: “No end in sight” describes the outlook at publication, rather than a dated prediction.
Neither “systemic failure” nor “revolution” supplies a shared test in this formulation.

entries.test: Public adoption, active-user, and revenue data for generative AI products other than ChatGPT would establish whether any had reached mass-market scale by publication.
entries.note: The ChatGPT exception must remain part of the test.
“Doesn't appear” explicitly qualifies the industry-wide profitability claim.

entries.test: Public financial trends and credible profitability plans available at publication would establish whether there were signs of the referenced companies ending cash burn.
entries.note: The source asserts an absence of present evidence, not a firm prediction of perpetual losses. “Any generative AI company” also loses the preceding exceptions.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures, unit economics, and cost-and-revenue projections would establish whether these companies had a financially credible route to profitability at publication.
entries.note: He rejects the claimed acceptability of this situation while asserting the underlying absence of a path to profitability.

entries.test: CoreWeave's 2024 financial statements and customer concentration disclosures would establish its losses, debt, revenue, and Microsoft/NVIDIA revenue share.

entries.note: The central interpretation is expressly tentative: “suggesting, I believe.” The customer ranking is separately factual.

entries.test: CoreWeave's public payment schedules, OpenAI revenue commitments, and alternative liquidity sources would establish whether paying its bills required and exhausted that revenue.
entries.note: The sentence awkwardly describes revenue being absorbed by obligations; its financial dependency has a plain reading.

entries.test: CoreWeave's 2025 cash-flow results and the contemporaneously reported revenue projection would test the $15 billion burn forecast and $4.6 billion projection.
entries.note: The surrounding text uses “lose” to mean cash burn, including capital expenditure.

entries.test: CoreWeave's capacity commitments, expansion financing plans, and DDTL 2.0 agreement would establish its financing needs and mandatory debt repayment provisions.
CoreWeave's public customer concentration, contracted backlog, liquidity, and lending covenants would establish its dependence on OpenAI payments.

entries.note: The proposition weakens “entire” buildout being in Core Scientific's hands to general dependence. The assertion about prior AI data centers is explicitly hedged.
The proposition omits the stated loan-term and market conditions on potential funding access. “May not” leaves that outcome probabilistic.
The source presents his inference about Microsoft's private wishes; the proposition turns it into an unqualified corporate decision.

entries.test: OpenAI's reported 2025 losses or cash burn on the basis used in the estimate would test the projected amount of as much as $14 billion.
entries.note: A numerical estimate is not automatically probability language; the source says “will.”
“Does not appear” qualifies the conclusion about SoftBank's financing capacity.

entries.test: OpenAI's public financial information and credible profitability projections would establish whether adequate SoftBank funding still left it without a viable route to profit.
entries.note: The concession does not turn the statement into a prediction conditional on future funding.

entries.test: Public evidence that the OpenAI deal proceeded as planned, together with CoreWeave's 2025 cash-flow statement, would test the conditional $15 billion burn forecast.
entries.note: The 2025 deadline has passed; the antecedent must also be checked.

entries.test: CoreWeave's disclosed liquidity, required expansion spending, loan covenants, and customer contract conditions would establish the claimed funding gap and dependencies.
OpenAI's reported 2025 losses, liquidity, fundraising, and CoreWeave payment obligations would test both the loss amount and the asserted dependence on new capital.
entries.note: The main assertion is a financing dependency supported by a dated loss forecast.

entries.test: OpenAI's publicly reported financial projections and explanations available at publication would establish its expected profitability date and stated route to it.
entries.note: This concerns reported company projections, not whether profitability will actually occur in 2030.

entries.test: Public SoftBank debt issuance outcomes, lender commentary, and credit-market analyses would test whether AI investor sentiment determines its access to borrowing.
entries.note: “How much” narrows borrowing ability to quantity, while “depend on” weakens “dictated by.”

entries.test: Public financial results and credible evidence of improving profitability available at publication would test the losses and asserted absence of evidence they could end.
entries.note: “All of these things” includes compute delivery and business expansion, not just funding.

entries.test: If SoftBank becomes unable to supply the described financing, public evidence of CoreWeave's and OpenAI's subsequent survival or business failure would test the predicted collapses.
entries.note: In context, “buckles” refers to failure of SoftBank's financing support.

entries.test: The companies' financing disclosures and continued operations through March 24, 2026 would establish whether maintaining the situation required raising tens of billions of dollars.
entries.note: The funding requirement is explicitly conditional on maintaining the situation for the next year.
The claim defines neither the relevant set of discussions nor what counts as fictional.
The proposition removes “I fear” from the broad economic claim. “Built our economy on top of NVIDIA” has no shared test, although spending and capacity withdrawals are factual.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures showing any enterprise other than NVIDIA earning profit from generative AI at publication would falsify the claim.
entries.note: This statement omits the Turing exception included earlier in the post.
“I fear” presents a possible adverse scenario rather than a firm expectation.
This is a judgment condemning optimism. The proposition drops the limiting phrase “at this point.”
